identification.summary: Cyberespionage group that ESET named MoustachedBouncer and describes as aligned with Belarusian government interests, targeting foreign embassies in Belarus [S1][S2]. Microsoft's naming mapping lists MoustachedBouncer as an alias of Storm-1125 [S6].
identification.firstObserved: ESET: active since at least 2014 [S2]. ESET lost track of the group in 2020 and saw it again in February 2022 per press summaries of the research [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-1125 (Belarus), with MoustachedBouncer as the other name per Microsoft's mapping file [S6]. Technical detail in this record comes from ESET's August 2023 research as published and as reported by press; no Microsoft-authored report on Storm-1125 was found in searches. ESET assesses with low confidence that the group collaborates with Winter Vivern; this is a separate cluster and is not merged here [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Belarus (alignment with Belarusian government interests, per ESET) [S2].
attribution.confidence: ESET assesses with medium confidence that the group is aligned with the interests of the Belarusian government [S1][S2]. No government attribution was found in searches.
attribution.basis: ESET cites the exclusive targeting of foreign embassies in Belarus and the likely use of ISP-level traffic interception inside Belarus, which ESET links to Belarus's lawful interception capability [S2][S5].

objectives: Espionage against diplomatic staff of foreign embassies in Belarus, collecting screenshots, audio and files from victims [S2][S3].

regions: Embassies of two European countries, one South Asian country and one African country, per ESET [S4]
targeting.notes: ESET says the group targets only foreign embassies in Belarus, including European ones, and identified four affected countries [S2][S4].

capabilities.summary: Two malware frameworks. NightClub, in use since 2014, is a modular C++ implant that exfiltrates over email using attacker-created free webmail accounts on Seznam.cz and Mail.ru, and ESET also saw DNS used by one plugin [S2]. Disco, in use since 2020, is a Go-based dropper-style framework paired with adversary-in-the-middle attacks, in which victims are redirected to a fake Windows Update page; ESET believes this happens at ISP level [S1][S2][S4]. Both frameworks support plugins including a screenshotter, audio recorder and file stealer [S2]. NightClub is used where ISP-level interception is not possible, for example when victims use an end-to-end encrypted VPN routed outside Belarus [S2]. Conference slides also list SMB shares as a C2 channel [S3].

campaigns.name: NightClub framework in use
campaigns.summary: ESET dates the earliest NightClub activity to 2014 [S2].

campaigns.name: Disco framework and ISP-level AitM
campaigns.summary: ESET reports Disco in use in parallel with NightClub from 2020, with the group likely using ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle attacks to serve a fake Windows Update page [S2][S4].

campaigns.name: Reappearance in ESET telemetry
campaigns.summary: Press summaries of ESET's research say ESET lost track of the group in 2020 and observed it again in February 2022 [S4].

campaigns.name: ESET public disclosure at Black Hat USA
campaigns.summary: ESET presented MoustachedBouncer at Black Hat USA 2023, naming four countries whose embassy staff were targeted and assessing low-confidence collaboration with Winter Vivern [S1][S2][S3].

diamond.adversary: Group ESET calls MoustachedBouncer, assessed with medium confidence as aligned with Belarusian government interests; Microsoft tracks it as Storm-1125 [S2][S6].
diamond.capability: NightClub (C++, email C2) and Disco (Go) frameworks with screenshot, audio and file-theft plugins; AitM fake Windows Update delivery [S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Attacker-created Seznam.cz and Mail.ru email accounts for NightClub exfiltration; DNS used by one plugin; ISP-level interception position inside Belarus assessed as likely [S2][S5].
diamond.victim: Staff of foreign embassies in Belarus; four countries identified (two European, one South Asian, one African) [S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on foreign diplomatic activity in Belarus, consistent with ESET's assessment of alignment with Belarusian government interests [S2].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints used by embassy staff, reliant on local Belarusian ISP connectivity; ISP lawful interception capability is the assessed enabler, and end-to-end VPNs routed outside Belarus push the actor to email-based NightClub [S2][S5].

gaps: No Microsoft-authored report on Storm-1125 was found; the Storm-1125 to MoustachedBouncer link rests on Microsoft's naming mapping file [S6].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is host-nation telecommunications (ISP links in Belarus) and diplomatic or deployed personnel endpoints reachable over that network [S2][S5]. STEP 2: The adversary can sit on the path of traffic inside Belarus (assessed, not confirmed), so users on local ISPs are exposed regardless of endpoint hygiene; encrypted VPNs routed outside the country force a fallback to email-based implants [S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is an AitM fake Windows Update lure leading to Disco, or NightClub where interception fails, then plugins for screenshots, audio and files, and exfiltration via webmail accounts [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against foreign diplomatic missions in Belarus. MDCOA is use of the same ISP-level position against military or exercise personnel transiting or deployed in the country or its region (analyst extrapolation, not reported). Candidate indicators: Windows Update prompts delivered over non-Microsoft hosts or invalid certificates on local ISP links, outbound SMTP/IMAP to Seznam.cz or Mail.ru from unexpected hosts, and unexpected screenshot or audio capture processes [S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track host-nation network risk for any personnel in Belarus or neighboring ISP environments and treat local ISP connectivity as untrusted. (2) Authorities: monitoring of diplomatic or partner networks falls to the host agency (for example State Department); coordinate rather than assume DoD authority. (3) Mission assurance: require trusted VPN routing outside the host country and verified software update channels; block consumer webmail egress from sensitive endpoints [S2]. (4) Coordination: share ESET-reported behaviors with partner embassies and allies through established intelligence-sharing channels, noting evidence is vendor-sourced with medium confidence [S2].
